planting.note: Tuck small divisions or nursery plugs into crevices of mortared or dry-stacked limestone walls and rockwork rather than open garden soil, since this fern is adapted to thin alkaline cracks rather than beds.

directions: This diminutive evergreen fern naturally roots in cracks of limestone and mortar walls, so recreate that niche with tufa, broken concrete, or limestone rubble rather than conventional border soil. Its small, leathery, blue-green fronds form tight tufts that tolerate drought once established but resent sitting in wet, heavy ground. Grow it in a shaded rock garden, between paving stones, or on an old masonry wall where lime leaches into the joints. Division is slow and plants are best left undisturbed for years once settled.

planting.note: Site divisions in shaded rock crevices or a well-drained gritty scree with acidic to neutral stone, as this spleenwort favors sharp drainage over rich garden loam.

directions: Black spleenwort gets its name from the glossy, near-black stipes that contrast with its dark green, triangular, finely divided evergreen fronds. In the wild it wedges its roots into shaded rock fissures and old walls, so a crevice garden or vertical rockery with sharp drainage suits it far better than a flat border. It is slow-growing and best treated as a specimen for a shaded alpine trough or stone wall rather than mass planting. Avoid winter waterlogging, which is its main cause of decline in cultivation.

planting.note: Plant in cool, shaded limestone scree or a crevice bed with constant air movement; this alpine fern struggles in summer heat and needs cool roots year-round.

directions: Green spleenwort is a small alpine and subarctic fern distinguished from its close relative maidenhair spleenwort by a bright green, unpigmented rachis rather than a dark one. It needs cool, humid conditions and calcareous rock crevices, making it a challenging but rewarding choice for a shaded alpine house, trough, or north-facing stone wall in cooler climates. Hot, humid summers are its main limitation, so gardeners outside its comfort zone should expect it to persist rather than thrive. Keep roots cool and constantly slightly moist, never waterlogged.

planting.note: Wedge small plants into vertical cracks of acidic rock such as granite or sandstone in a shaded scree or wall, since this fern needs sharp drainage and will rot in ordinary bedded soil.

directions: Forked spleenwort is one of the oddest-looking hardy ferns, with narrow, grass-like fronds repeatedly forked into thin, dark green segments that bear little resemblance to a typical frond outline. It is a true crevice specialist, rooting in narrow vertical cracks of acidic rock where almost nothing else can establish, and it resists cultivation in conventional soil. Best grown in a shaded rock garden or alpine trough with acidic grit, it is a collector's novelty rather than a mainstream garden plant. Patience is required, as establishment from divisions is slow and uneven.
